A KMS key policy alone is not sufficient for cross-account use: cross-account access requires permission both in the key policy of the KMS key and in an IAM policy in the external user's account.
The key policy must give the external account (or users and roles in it) permission to use the KMS key, and IAM policies in the external account must delegate those key policy permissions to its users and roles; neither policy alone is sufficient.
Cross-account permission is effective only for these operations: cryptographic operations, CreateGrant, DescribeKey, GetKeyRotationStatus, GetPublicKey, ListGrants, RetireGrant, and RevokeGrant; permissions for other operations given to a user in a different account have no effect.

For SSE-KMS, if you want to use a customer managed key, you must create a symmetric encryption customer managed key before configuring SSE-KMS, then specify that existing key when configuring SSE-KMS for your bucket.
Objects encrypted using SSE-KMS with AWS managed keys can't be shared cross-account; if you need to share SSE-KMS data cross-account, you must use a customer managed key from AWS KMS.
If you want to grant cross-account access to your S3 objects, use a customer managed key, whose policy you can configure to allow access from another account.
When specifying a customer managed KMS key, AWS recommends using a fully qualified KMS key ARN, because using a KMS key alias instead causes AWS KMS to resolve the key within the requester's account, which can result in data encrypted with a key belonging to the requester rather than the bucket owner.

When you configure server-side encryption using AWS KMS (SSE-KMS), you can configure your buckets to use S3 Bucket Keys for SSE-KMS; using a bucket-level key for SSE-KMS can reduce AWS KMS request costs by up to 99 percent by decreasing the request traffic from Amazon S3 to AWS KMS.
When a bucket is configured to use an S3 Bucket Key for SSE-KMS on new objects, AWS KMS generates a bucket-level key that is used to create unique data keys for objects in the bucket.
The S3 Bucket Key is used for a time-limited period within Amazon S3, which further reduces the need for Amazon S3 to make requests to AWS KMS to complete encryption operations.
